Regarding the mountains, Ibn Kathir and others report that they were fixed so the earth would not shake with its people.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a sequence of blessings Allah bestowed on the earth after creating the heaven. Allah set the mountains firmly in the ground, meaning He anchored them and made them like pegs that keep the earth from shaking with its inhabitants. The passage moves from the creation of the sky to the arrangement of the earth and its resources, to show that the One who can do this can also raise the dead. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur agree that irsa means to make firm and stable, and that the mountains serve to steady the earth. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite a report attributed to 'Ali about the earth quivering before the mountains were placed, which al-Tabari transmits with his chain. Az-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the word al-jibal is read in both the accusative and the nominative. The exegetes also observe that mentioning water and pasture before the mountains reflects God's care for food and drink. On the order of creation, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the earth was created before the sky but spread out after it, while az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur argue that the word after marks rank rather than time, and that ba'd can mean 'together with'. What they share is the recognition of a terrestrial world prepared for life.

The commentators explain that the phrase "a provision for you and your cattle" means that God did what is listed, spreading the earth, bringing forth water and pasture, and fixing the mountains, as enjoyment and benefit for people and their livestock for a set time. The passage lists the blessings of creation to show God's power to resurrect. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir take matā' as enjoyment or provision, in the accusative as a verbal equivalent or as an object of purpose. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan treat the bringing forth of water and pasture as an explanation of the spreading and levelling of the earth, with the mountains holding it steady for its people. As for the "greatest calamity" that follows, the commentators agree it is the Day of Resurrection or the second blast of the trumpet. Al-Hasan identifies it as the second blast, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak say it is the Resurrection itself, and al-Tabari notes that the word denotes a disaster that overwhelms all others. On "after that" in "and the earth, after that, He spread it out", Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the earth was created before the sky but spread out after it, whereas Mujahid and others read "after" as "together with", and some as "before". All agree these verses establish resurrection and recompense, and God knows best what He intended.

The commentators explain that "al-Tamma al-Kubra" is the great calamity that rises above and overwhelms every other calamity, and that it most often refers to the Day of Resurrection. Most agree that it is the Resurrection itself, as Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak report, and they explain the name by the fact that it engulfs everything dreadful. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note that some take it to be the second blast of the trumpet, which brings about the resurrection, following al-Hasan and another report from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Qasim ibn al-Walid and Mujahid identify it as the moment when the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of the Fire to the Fire, while al-Mawardi reports that al-Rabi' took it to be the Hour itself. Al-Sam'ani and al-Razi recall the linguistic sense of the root, meaning to rise above, overpower or bury. The following verse, which says that man will remember what he strove for and that Hellfire will be displayed to whoever sees it, is presented by most as an explanation of that day; al-Tabari and al-Baghawi add that the Fire will be uncovered. The reading "li-man tara" in the second person is noted by Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, who take it as an address to the Prophet or as referring to the Fire, while the majority read "li-man yara". Several scholars do not deliver a firm verdict on these differences.

This passage describes the Day of Judgment, which many commentators call "the Great Calamity", the catastrophe that overwhelms all other catastrophes. The exegetes explain that on that day a person will recall everything he did in this world, good and bad, and that Hellfire will be displayed to whoever sees it. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others report several meanings of the Calamity: for al-Hasan it is the second blast of the trumpet that brings resurrection; for Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Dahhak it is one of the names of the Last Day; for al-Qasim ibn al-Walid and Mujahid it is the moment when the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire are led to their abodes. Linguistically, the word denotes what covers and overwhelms everything else. The commentators agree that Hellfire is made visible, but differ on who sees it: Ibn Kathir, al-Jaza'iri and others say every onlooker; al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya say the disbeliever sees it with its torments, while al-Qurtubi adds that the believer sees it to recognise the value of his blessing. Some read "for the one you see", referring to the Prophet or to Hellfire. The text then contrasts the rebel who preferred the worldly life, whose refuge is Hellfire, with the one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from its desires, whose refuge is Paradise. Muqatil and al-Mawardi explain that this fearful person is one who, about to disobey, remembers his reckoning and refrains.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the great calamity arrives, the catastrophe that overwhelms all others. They differ on what it is: al-Hasan says it is the second blast of the trumpet, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak say it is the Resurrection itself, while al-Qasim ibn al-Walid and Mujahid say it is the moment when the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of the Fire to the Fire. On the linguistic sense, al-Mubarrad explains that it is a calamity that cannot be withstood. All agree that on that day a person will recall what he did, good and bad, and that Hell will be displayed plainly to every beholder. Muqatil says the covering will be lifted so that all creatures can look at it, whereas al-Razi and Ibn Kathir hold that every person with sight will see it, the believers passing by it. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the reading with ta, "li-man tara", may refer to Hell or to the Prophet. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi add that the disbeliever sees it with its torments, and some say the believer sees it so he may recognise the value of his blessing. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Sa'di conclude that whoever transgresses and prefers the life of this world will have Hell as his abode, while whoever fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire will have Paradise as his abode.

This part of the verse divides people on the Day of Resurrection into two groups. Whoever transgressed and rebelled against God, preferring the life of this world to the Hereafter, will have the Blazing Fire as his abode. Al-Tabari explains transgression (taghā) as disobedience and arrogance toward worshipping God, and Mujahid simply as disobedience. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya add that it means crossing the limits a person should respect, and that preferring this world can mean denying the Hereafter.

Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir hold that the verse applies generally to every disbeliever, though some reports say it was revealed about an-Nadr ibn al-Harith or others. Al-Razi sees two corruptions here: one of the theoretical faculty, since the transgressor fails to recognise his own lowliness before God, and one of the practical faculty, loving this world. He holds that whoever has both reaches the extreme of corruption, citing the hadith that love of the world is the root of every sin. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di define transgression as going beyond the bounds of the law, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that preferring worldly goods is blameworthy only when it costs one the goods of the Hereafter.

The commentators agree that the answer to the conditional "When the Great Calamity comes" is omitted, and that the "as for" particle introduces the division of people into two groups. Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari take "the Blazing Fire is his refuge" as the answer itself, while the Basran grammarians supply an implied pronoun and the Kufan grammarians treat the article as standing in for it.

Set against this is the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from its desires. Al-Tabari takes this fear to be dread of being questioned on the Day of Judgment, while Mujahid and al-Mawardi understand it as the fear that makes a person stop from sin at the moment of temptation. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that desire is an inclination of the soul, and that the Qur'an generally uses the word in a negative sense.

This part of the verse states that whoever transgresses the bounds set by God, rebels against His command and prefers the pleasures of this world to the Hereafter will have Hellfire as his abode, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, the two Jalals and al-Shawkani explain. Al-Tabari reports from Mujahid that tughyan means disobedience, while Ibn Atiyya defines it as crossing the limits a person should stop at. Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn take preferring the life of this world to mean giving oneself to desires and neglecting preparation for the Hereafter. Al-Razi links transgression to a corruption of the theoretical faculty and preference for this world to a corruption of the practical faculty, which he considers the gravest form of corruption. Commentators generally contrast this person with the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from its desires, whose abode will be Paradise. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan describe the dispute between the Basran grammarians, who posit an omitted pronoun in 'al-ma'wa', and the Kufans, who read the definite article as a replacement for the possessive. On the occasion of revelation, most cite Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and his brother, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith or Abu Jahl, but Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi hold that the ruling is general, since the lesson lies in the wording rather than the specific cause. Several commentators also cite a hadith, which Qurtubi notes is attributed to Ka'b al-Ahbar, that whoever prefers this world will have his concerns scattered by God.

This part of the verse states that whoever transgresses the bounds set by God and prefers the enjoyments of this world to the Hereafter will have Hellfire as his abode, that is, his final destination. Al-Tabari explains that tughyan means disobedience and rebellion against God, and that al-Jahim is the fire of God known by that name, the place to which this man will return on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir adds that his food will be zaqqum and his drink boiling water. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain that the definite article in al-ma'wa stands in for a possessive pronoun, meaning his abode; Zamakhshari justifies this by noting that the rebel is clearly the owner of that abode. The grammarians of Basra hold that the pronoun is implied and omitted, while those of Kufa treat the article as a substitute for it. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim relate this conduct to attachment to worldly life and to desire as a source of disobedience. Ibn 'Ashur clarifies that what is blamed is preferring this life over the Hereafter, not enjoying worldly goods that do not cost one the goods of the Hereafter. The next verse sets against this the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from its desires, whose abode will be Paradise. The commentators also transmit various occasions of revelation, notably linked to Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and his brother, but the scope of the verse remains general.

This part of the verse contrasts the rebel with the one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from its desires; for him, Paradise is the abode. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand this fear as the dread of standing before God for judgment, while Mujahid places it in this life, when a person is about to commit a sin and refrains from it. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas agrees with the reading of the Day of Judgment. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir present these two attributes as the opposite of those of the people of Hell: fear opposes rebellion, and restraining the self opposes preferring the worldly life. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the blame falls only on preferring this world over the Hereafter, not on lawfully enjoying its goods. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi define hawa as the soul's inclination toward its desires, and restraining it as turning it away from what displeases God. Some commentators report that the verse was revealed about Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, though this is not presented as a general rule, and al-Tabari mentions no occasion of revelation. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes the soul at peace, the self-reproaching soul and the soul that commands evil, and concludes that these are one soul described by different qualities.

This part of the verse sets against each other two destinies: the one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from its desires will find Paradise as his dwelling and place of return, while the one who transgressed and preferred the life of this world will find the Blazing Fire as his refuge. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi, agree that al-ma'wa means the place where one retreats and remains. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the standing before the Lord as the reckoning and recompense on the Day of Judgment, while Mujahid, followed by Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Qayyim, understands the fear as the restraint in this world that stops a person from sinning at the moment of temptation. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim note that these two qualities oppose the two traits of the people of the Fire. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes the commanding soul, the self-reproaching soul and the tranquil soul, and holds that restraining the soul from its desires requires calling it to account. Al-Qurtubi reports that Sahl and others considered abandoning desire the key to Paradise. Several commentators, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, relate that the mention of desire refers to specific people such as Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, whereas al-Tabari does not mention this. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi read the verse as a general rule for every believer who fears his Lord. These readings remain side by side, and none is presented as the only valid meaning.

This verse reports that the unbelievers asked when the Hour will come, using the word mursaha. The commentators explain it in two ways. Al-Farra, cited by al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi, compares its establishment to a ship coming to rest at anchor, meaning the moment it will take place. Abu Ubayda, followed by al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, understands it as its final end or resting place. Al-Baghawi and al-Alusi take it to mean its appearance and fixing.

There is broad agreement that the question concerns the exact time and that this knowledge belongs to God alone, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy stress. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Gabriel, in which the Prophet says that the one asked knows no more than the one asking. Ibn Abbas, reported by al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi, held that the question was asked in mockery, and Ibn Ashur sees it as a way of denying that the Hour will come.

The phrase fima anta min dhikraha has been read in different ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Juzayy and al-Razi report the account of Aisha that the Prophet kept asking about the Hour until this verse was revealed and he stopped. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari take it as asking what business he has in naming its time. Al-Mawardi gives two possible meanings, and Ibn Ashur notes that the Prophet's task was to warn, which benefits only those who fear the Hour.

The idolaters asked the Prophet ﷺ, mockingly, when the Hour would come. The answer is that its knowledge belongs to God alone, so the Prophet is not asked to name its time or to keep speaking of it. The commentators agree on the core meaning: what concern is it of yours to mention its time? Its final knowledge rests with your Lord. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the Prophet often spoke about the Hour and asked about it until this verse made him stop, as Aisha is cited as saying. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda explain that (mursaha) means its establishment or its end, like a ship coming to rest at harbour. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that (fima) either expresses wonder at the Prophet's insistence or rejects the question itself, and he notes that the pause after (fima) can separate the two sentences. All agree that the warning is for those who fear the Hour, though some extend it to everyone responsible, since fear is what benefits from warning. The reading (mundhiru) with tanwin, attributed to Abu Ja'far, and the construct form followed by most readers are both accepted by al-Tabari. Finally, the commentators explain that on the day they see the Hour, the deniers will think they lingered only an evening or a morning, meaning that earthly life will seem very short to them, according to Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the question of the disbelievers about when the Hour will come: knowledge of its appointed time belongs to God alone, and the Prophet is not charged with fixing its date, but only with warning those who fear it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy understand 'muntahaha' as the limit of knowledge of it, which rests with God alone. Al-Tabari adds, on the report of Aisha, that the Prophet stopped asking about the Hour once this verse was revealed. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan explain that 'mursaha' means its settling or arrival, and that 'fima' may be a rebuke, meaning 'why this question?'. Ibn Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud also allow that the word denotes the final resting place of the Hour. Several authors, including al-Mawardi and al-Razi, stress that no one knows it, not even angels or prophets, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Gabriel to that effect. On recitation, al-Tabari considers the readings 'mundhirun' with tanwin and 'mundhiru man' without it to be two valid, well-known readings. For 'lam yalbathu illa 'ashiyyatan aw duhaha', al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir read it as a depiction of how short life in this world will seem to people, while the Tafsir al-Muyassar specifies the interval from midday to sunset, or from sunrise to midday.

The commentators explain that this verse comes in the context of the mocking question of the disbelievers about when the Hour will come. God tells His Messenger that knowledge of the Hour belongs to God alone and that his task is only to warn, not to fix the date. The apparent meaning the exegetes adopt is that you are only a warner to those who fear it, and you do not know its time. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Prophet asked about the Hour very often until these verses were revealed, which Ibn Kathir links to the hadith of Gabriel in which the Prophet says the one asked knows no more than the asker. All agree that knowledge of the Hour is with God and that only those who fear it benefit from the warning, although al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note that the warning is general for every responsible person. On the reading, most read the word as an annexation, while Abu Ja'far and others read it with tanwin. Al-Tabari judges that both readings are well known and correct. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan consider the tanwin the original form and the annexation a lightening. For the final phrase, most commentators, such as al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn, take it to mean that people will feel their life in this world was very short, while others, such as Qatada, take it as the time spent in the graves. Al-Farra' explains that 'evening or morning' refers to a single day.

This verse in Surat al-Nazi'at describes the state of those who deny the Hour on the day they witness it: it will seem to them that they lingered, in the world or in their graves, only for an evening or a morning, a very short part of a day. The commentators agree that the aim is to reduce the length of their stay and to make worldly life seem small in their eyes when faced with the terror of the resurrection. Al-Farra', followed by al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, explains that joining the morning to the evening refers to the morning of that same day, citing an Arabic line of poetry. Al-Razi argues that the two moments belong to one day, which is enough to justify the annexation, and that the rhyme also supports it. Ibn 'Abbas, according to a report from al-Dahhak, takes it to mean a single day. Ibn Kathir defines the evening as the span from midday to sunset and the morning as the span from sunrise to midday. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud read the phrase as a comparison with someone who stayed only briefly. Al-Tabari, quoting Qatada, speaks of how worldly life appears to those who have seen the hereafter. In the surrounding verses, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir link the unbelievers' questions about the Hour to their demand for precise dates, and note that the Prophet's role is only to warn those who fear it, since its exact time belongs to God alone.
